title.narrative: Världsbanken Global Water Security & Sanitation Partnership 2022-2025
World Bank Global Water Security & Sanitation Partnership 2022-2025

description.narrative:
The Global Water Security and Sanitation Partnership (GWSP) is a global co-financing fund at the World Bank, housed under and integrated into Water Global Practice (Water GP). With a poverty focus, GWSP supports countries to achieve SDG 6- a water secure world for all. Inclusion is a special theme to ensure and monitor that efforts promote participation and requirements of vulnerable groups, including people living with disabilities.
GWSP operates in the water and sanitation sector, with water resource management and with sustainable water use in agriculture.
GWSP has country presence in a large number of countries and is a reputable actor for global knowledge production and dissemination with opportunities for international as well as national policy influence. Through the close the connection to the World Bank's operations for lending, GWSP has the opportunity to catalyze funding to implement plans and programs.
In addition to GWSP being able to influence loans so that plans and initiatives can be realized and scaled up, the close connection to the World Bank's loan operations enables GWSP to contribute to the design of loans that are of a higher quality and better integrate the perspective of poor people, equality and inclusion and the environment - and climate aspects.
Sida assesses that GWSP's work has contributed and continues to contribute to advancing climate adaptation through, for example, initiatives for water reservoirs with multiple purposes (multipurpose), management and handling of catchment areas, resilience against drought and to emission reductions through, for example, nature-based solutions that integrate green and gray infrastructure , for example in sewage treatment. Many efforts thereby also contribute to disaster risk reduction.
The World Bank's system for environmental integration has been assessed as well developed by Sida centrally. GWSP's work, mainly in the water resources part and water for agriculture, has a direct positive impact on environmental effects, including on biodiversity. Through GWSP's support, the environmental perspective on, for example, World Bank loans for related infrastructure is strengthened. GWSP's work in water supply and sewage also contributes positively to reduced environmental impact, but that is not the primary aim, which is rather increased access to safe water and sanitation.
The effort involves a lot of private sector collaboration, partly with the aim of promoting private investment.
Based on established progress for eg gender equality and conflict, from the mid-term evaluation and the updated strategy, Sida assesses that for all perspectives, there are overall goals and a structural framework for how the perspectives should be addressed and integrated.
GWSP has a system for measuring the number of interventions that include gender equality work, which requires that the intervention has a logical flow from analysis, to activities and results frameworks that address inequality. The goal that 80% of initiatives should be marked by gender equality has so far been exceeded every year.

The Global Water Security and Sanitation Partnership (GWSP) är en global samfinansieringsfond på Världsbanken, huserad under och integrerad i Water Global Practice (Water GP), som utifrån ett fattigdomsfokus verkar för att stödja länder att uppnå SDG 6- en vattensäker värld för alla. Inkludering är ett särskilt tema för att säkerställa och mäta att insatser främjar deltagande och behov för utsatta grupper inklusive personer som lever med funktionsnedsättningar.
GWSP verkar inom vatten och sanitetssektorn, med vattenresurshantering samt med hållbar vattenanvändning inom jordbruk. GWSP har landnärvaro i ett stort antal länder och är en ansedd aktör för global kunskapsspridning med möjligheter till internationell så väl som nationell policypåverkan. Genom den nära kopplingen till Världsbankens verksamhet för utlåning har GWSP möjlighet att katalysera finansiering till att implementera planer och program.
Utöver att GWSP kan influera lån så att planer och initiativ kan realiseras och skalas upp möjliggör den nära kopplingen till låneverksamheten att GWSP i sin tur även bidrar till utformningen av lånen som får en högre kvalitet och bättre integrerar fattiga människors perspektiv, jämställdhet och inkludering samt miljö- och klimataspekter.
Sida bedömer att GWSPs arbete har bidragit och fortsatt bidrar till att avancera klimatanpassning genom t.ex insatser för vattenreservoarer med flera syften (multipurpose), förvaltning och hantering av avrinningsområden, resiliens mot torka och till utsläppsminskningar genom exempelvis naturbaserade lösningar som integrera grön och grå infrastruktur, exempelvis inom avloppshantering. Många insatser bidrar därigenom också till klimatriskreducering.
Världsbankens system för miljöintegrering har av Sida centralts bedömts väl utvecklat. GWSPs arbete, främst inom vattenresursdelen samt vatten för jordbruk har direkt positiv bäring på miljöeffekter inklusive för biologisk mångfald. Genom GWSPs stöd stärks miljöperspektivet på exempelvis Världsbankslån för relaterad infrastruktur. GWSPs arbete inom vattenförsörjning och avlopp bidrar också positivt till minskad miljöpåverkan, men det är inte främsta syftet, vilket snarere är ökad tillgång till säkert vatten och sanitet.
Insatsen innefattar mycket privatsektorssamarbete, delvis med mål att främja privata investeringar.
Utifrån konstaterade framsteg för exempelvis jämställdhet och konflikt samt utifrån halvtidsutvärderingen och den uppdaterade strategin bedömer Sida att det för samtliga perspektiv finns övergripande mål samt strukturella ramverk för hur perspektiven ska adresseras och integreras.
GWSP har ett system för att mäta antal insatser som inkluderar jämställdhetsarbete, vilket kräver att insatsen har ett logiskt flöde från analys, till aktiviteter och resultatramverk som adresserar ojämställdhet. Målet om att 80 % av insatser ska vara jämställdhetsmarkerade har hittills överskridits alla år.

The overall objective of the GWSP, expressed in their newly updated strategy Global Water Security and Sanitation Partnership Strategy update 2022, is to aid governments to achieve Sustainable Development Goal 6, a water secure world for all, by sustaining water resources, delivering services and building resilience.
Through generating relevant knowledge and analytics and strengthening the sectors enabling environment, the GWSP aims to contribute to the World Banks twin goals to "end extreme poverty and promote shared growth". The focus lies on providing technical support and strengthen systems while leveraging World Bank Group resources, domestic resources as well as other private investments for well-designed investments and efficient implementation of WASH-services, Water Resource management and climate resilient agriculture. The expectation is impacts from the supporting work of GWSP together with financing of infrastructure from other sources.
The GWSP aims to influence three thematic areas (referred to as business lines) of the Water GP; Water Supply and Sanitation (WSS), Water Resource Management (WRM), and Water in Agriculture (WiA).
The thematic areas are addressed by focusing on one or more of these five priority themes (sustainability, inclusion, institutions, financing and resilience). Work is carried out on global, regional, national and sub-national level.
A comprehensive results framework that measures different types of step wise improvements have been developed. The full results framework is presented in the annual report published on the World Banks/GWSP's webpage.
Expected results are partly the type/amount of knowledge products och technical assistance that GWSP will produce or provide. For example, outputs in the form of development of policies, strategies, regulatory frameworks, development of knowledge products, strengthening of water sector actors etc.
The knowledge products and technical assistance is then to contribute to improved and financed projects. Expected results also includes impact of GWSP on these projects, measured both as amount of funds that are leveraged and the design of the projects, such as for example inclusion of gender consideration, projects that promote sustainable and efficient water use or projects with an explicit focus on leveraging private finance.
The above expected results are then in their turn expected to contribute to the following targets: (Cumulative target range for 2023-2030 of a selection of expected results):
People with access to improved water sources: 103.2 - 119.1 million
People with access to improved sanitation: 67.38 - 77.6 million
Health centers and schools with access to improved water and sanitation service: 11.000-15.000
Area with new/improved irrigation services: 5.84 - 7.62 million hectares
People in areas covered by water risk mitigation measures (flooding/drought): 33.1 - 40 million
Institutions with WRM monitoring systems: 176 - 192
Area under sustainable land/water management practices: 8 - 9.4 million hectares

title.narrative: Avtal om stöd till GWSP 2022 och 2023
Beslut om stöd till GWSP 2022 och 2023

description.narrative:
In FY24, GWSP disbursed $30.2 million and had an active portfolio of 243 activities.
Results in relation to the three thematic areas:
Improving water resources management
GWSP financing provided analytical and diagnostic support to 23 country-level climate and development reports in fiscal year 2024. In addition, GWSP provided technical expertise support to help design Bank projects so that all new lending for investments in the water sector is in line with the Bank's commitments under the Paris Agreement.
GWSP has provided technical expertise to help design Bank projects so that all new lending for investments in the water sector is in line with the Bank's commitments under the Paris Agreement. This support has helped ensure that 68% of new World Bank lending has a positive impact on climate change, and that 100% of projects have at least one climate-related indicator in their results framework.
Examples of GWSP technical assistance include, in Burkina Faso, the World Bank's strenghtening of dams vulnerable to flooding, more drought-resistant irrigation for farmers, installation of climate early warning systems, and investments in vegetation cover restoration to reduce erosion and runoff. In Cambodia, the Bank has contributed to strengthening climate resilience by increasing access to piped water in water-scarce regions vulnerable to droughts and floods, as well as improving sanitation services in areas often affected by extreme climate conditions.
GWSP has provided advice and technical assistance to various infrastructure projects financed by the Bank. In 2024, GWSP advised on projects representing loans totalling USD 44.8bn, of which USD 9.3bn was for new loan projects. Among the lending projects influenced by GWSP, representing commitments of more than USD 2.8bn, were six conflict-affected countries (Burkina Faso, Central African Republic, Comoros, Ethiopia, Nigeria and Timor-Leste) and one conflict-sensitive region (Eastern and Southern Africa).
The World Bank Group's Water Resources Management Initiative focuses on reducing hydro-climatic risks - particularly from floods and droughts - thereby increasing the capacity to cope with more variable water flows and improving sustainable water management at local, national and transboundary river basin levels. GWSP funds critical analytical work that helps to achieve such outcomes in water management. In Europe and Central Asia, GWSP has helped develop a new agile approach to water security diagnostics. In-depth country-level water security analyses were carried out in Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia, and more comprehensive reports were produced for eight additional countries. The rapid diagnostic processes allow for productive dialogues at country level and the identification of specific challenges. In Albania, for example, discussions led to the government securing EU funding to address dam safety and to develop nationwide sanitation plans.
GWSP support also enabled the Bank to strengthen its expertise in nature-based solutions (NBS) for climate resilience. In Fiji, NBS training helped a Bank team design a proposed project to improve water quality in selected catchments through approaches that include constructed wetlands for wastewater treatment. In addition, GWSP supported the Bank's efforts to promote sediment assessment and mitigation in reservoirs and dams in Central Asia.
Climate-Resilient Irrigation
GWSP has supported results in climate-resilient irrigation projects. In Nigeria, GWSP funds supported training for officials responsible for the country's water policy in river basins to understand, prioritise and plan for dam safety and maintenance, helping to ensure long-term food security. In India, GWSP supported the training of staff at the Ministry of Water Resources and state governments to use two different remote sensing tools: one to assess which irrigation systems are working and one to assess irrigation performance. In Indonesia, where GWSP funded research for a bank project that improved irrigation services and promoted climate-smart agricultural practices, farmers' incomes have increased by 25 per cent.
Water Supply and Sanitation
In the Lake Victoria basin, GWSP has supported five countries to reduce discharges and pollution into the lake. In collaboration with the organisation Water & Sanitation for the Urban Poor, GWSP has supported inclusive work to develop the Lakewide Inclusive Sanitation Strategy, which was adopted by the Lake Victoria Ministerial Council in February 2024. GWSP has also funded analyses of the sanitation situation in 57 urban areas in five countries to identify hot spots. The results have formed the basis of action plans for four cities in Kenya, Rwanda, Uganda and Tanzania that identify investments for improved sanitation.
The Lusaka Sanitation Project ended in FY24 after improving sanitation for approximately 345,000 people (50 percent of them women), exceeding the targeted number of beneficiaries. Notably, the project contributed to greater sanitation access in peri-urban areas, where most of the citys poor reside. In addition, the project improved fecal sludge management in Lusaka and increased the sewerage network and connections to it. One result was lower rates of waterborne diseases.
The GWSP-funded Water Supply and Sanitation Sector Diagnostic highlighted inefficiencies hindering the government of Zambia's goal of achieving universal access to water and sanitation by 2030. The findings indicated the need for a shift from investing in infrastructure to improving efficiency, reducing nonrevenue water, and enhancing financial viability through operational improvements and technological innovations. The diagnostics findings and recommendations have been instrumental in developing a new project in Zambia to strengthen commercial utilities by improving their operational and financial efficiencies.
GWSP also give "just in time support" to countries. In Burundi and Democratic Republic of Congo where technical support was given for project design for water supply, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) in schools and health care facilities. In Columbia support was given to implment "best practises" in WASH implementation for schools and health centers, reviewing national standards and developing a strategy to pilot institutional WASH facilities in participating municipalities.
Reporting against the GWSP results framework:
GWSP indicators are grouped into three blocks.
- Block A looks at the multiyear knowledge and technical assistance activities supported by GWSP.
- Block B considers how GWSP-supported knowledge and technical assistance has influenced newly approved and active World Bank lending operations in terms of design and outcomes.
- Block C includes qualitative and quantitative assessments of the influence and impact of knowledge and technical assistance on lending operations of the Global Department for Water in nine priority countries, based on agreed-upon indicators, at intervals over the life of GWSP.
Examples of results under Block A Knowledge and Technical Assistance:
-31 countries (compared with 26 countries in FY 23) were supported to develop policies and strategies that strengthen the sustainable management of water resources and built infrastructure assets.
-13 countries (11 in FY 23) were supported to improve the financial viability and creditworthiness of their water sector institutions.
-13 countries (8 in FY 23) were supported to develop policies/strategies to enhance social inclusion of women, persons with disabilities or other excluded groups in the management of water resources or service delivery.
-34 countries (28 in FY 23) were supported to strengthen the capacity of their water-related institutions for managing water resources or service delivery.
-31 countries (12 in FY 23) were supported to develop policies, strategies or regulatory frameworks to improve financial viability.
Examples of results under Block B Reporting on Portfolio Shifts (GWSP influence on lending)
In FY24, total approved financing for water, led by the Water Department, was $3.64 billion, almost a billion less than in FY23. This financing corresponded to 22 projects spanning GWSPs three main business lines: water supply and sanitation (11 projects), water resources management (7 projects), and climate-resilient irrigation (4 projects).
In FY24, projects improved or maintained their performance against 11 of 14 Block B1 indicators tracking GWSPs influence in the design of new water lending. Under the theme of sustainability, all 22 projects approved in FY24 scored positively against the indicator documenting the inclusion of measures that promote sustainable and efficient water use. Projects have not yet met the FY30 targets for 4 of 11 indicators under the themes of inclusion, financing, and resilience, but they are showing progress. In FY24, all 22 approved water projects promoted sustainable and efficient water use.
A shortfall last year was the number of project with explicit focus on leveraging private capital which was only 8 for the FY 23, compared to the yearly target of 20. This was addressed though different measures, which were presented to the donor partnership council in February 2024, and the results for FY 24 was 40 projects.
The result of the lending per overarching objective: (Average target range/ year for the peroid 2023-2030 of a selection of expected results):
People with access to improved water sources: 17.24 million ( 12.0-14.9)
People with access to improved sanitation: 4.13 million (8.42-9.7)
Health centers and schools with access to improved water and sanitation service: 5404 units ( 1377-1875)
People in areas covered by water risk mitigation measures (flooding/drought): 16.37 million (4.1-5)
Institutions with WRM monitoring systems: 24 (22-24)
Area under sustainable land/water management practices: 2.9 millions of hectares (1.0-1.2)
The number of people provided with access to improved water in FY24 was 17.24 million, 16 percent above the upper bound of the yearly target range. This over-performance was mainly due to results reported by the Karachi Water and Sewerage Services Improvement Project in Pakistan, which provided access to 7.26 million additional people in FY24, exceeding its own target.
The number of schools and health centers with access to improved water and sanitation services increased from 2559 in FY23 to 5404 in FY24.
The shortfall of the sanitation work is an effect of timing of completion. The yearly average of sanitation achievement is still above the yearly target. 54 percent of the people provided with access to sanitation in FY24 through World Bank projects were in IDA-eligible countries.
13 percent of total results were in countries affected by fragility and conflict (Burkina Faso, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Guinea-Bissau, Haiti, Iraq, Mali, Mozambique, Nigeria, Papua New Guinea, the Solomon Islands, Somalia, and Yemen).
Results examples from Block C countries:
With GWSP support, Vietnam has strengthened its legal and policy framework for water security, shifting the focus from policy development to implementation through a national, transboundary and inter-ministerial approach. The support has led to the implementation of key World Bank recommendations for a more sustainable water system and for improving the safety of dams and reservoirs. GWSP has also supported the development of the Mekong Delta Regional Plan, approved in 2023; the revision of Vietnam's National Law on Water Resources, adopted in 2023; the development of the law's guiding decree, which focuses on the economic valuation of water; the preparation of a roadmap for the establishment of a national water resources information and decision support system; and the development of a national investment programme for river revitalization. Furthermore, the GWSP supported the development of a new law on water supply and drainage aimed at ensuring water supply in urban and rural settlements.
GWSP has supported improved access to water and sanitation and integrated water resources management (IWRM) in Uganda under the World Bank-funded Integrated Water Management and Development Project (IWMDP), a USD 280 million project for the period 2018-2026, focusing on the vulnerable northern and eastern regions of Uganda and the districts hosting large numbers of refugees, as well as areas with low coverage of water supply and sanitation. GWSP has contributed to Uganda's national groundwater assessment and to the development of 66 watershed and water source protection plans. The targets for the number of protection plans were comfortably met. GWSP also provided advisory support to the Ministry of Water and Environment on its Water and Environment Information System. The system was installed and operationalized in 2024 and rolled out to three of the four regional water management offices. The system is expected to become the Ugandan water sector's main management information.
GWSP has supported Bolivia in the preparation of a USD 173 million sustainable irrigation project that was approved for IBRD financing in 2024. GWSP has supported the development of various tools, including for calculating optimal irrigated areas, for assessing the vulnerability of dams to sedimentation, and for analyzing the conditions for growing and selling various agricultural products. It has also contributed to the development of three river basin plans.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
